plan: Informational essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000015) on a volunteer sea-star survey, with past-perfect tense, an appositive fragment and a keep-sentence item; E014-09 resubmitted with its arguable colon choice replaced.

passages.title: Counting Sea Stars
passages.text:
Twice a month, during the lowest tides, a group of volunteers gathers on the rocks below Point Harlan with clipboards and measuring tapes. They are counting sea stars{{1|, the}} task is slower than it sounds. Each animal must be found, measured, and checked for signs of the wasting disease that killed millions of sea stars along the Pacific coast beginning in 2013.

The survey was started by Lena Ashby, a marine biologist {{2|which}} teaches at the community college nearby. When the disease first appeared, she realized that no one had kept careful records of how many sea stars lived at the point before the outbreak. {{3|Without those numbers, it was impossible to say how much had been lost.}} She resolved that if another outbreak came, there would be a baseline.

The volunteers range from retirees to high school students. Most had never {{4|seen, a sea star}} up close before joining, and Ashby trains them in a single afternoon. Two people looking at the same pool, she has found, rarely count exactly the same number of animals. {{5|For this reason,}} she insists that every count be checked by a second person.

The work has already paid off. In 2021, the volunteers noticed young sea stars in pools where none had been seen for years. Because the survey had begun well before the recovery, Ashby had the numbers to measure it. By the time she published her report in 2023, the number of juveniles {{6|has tripled}} since the first sightings{{7|. A}} finding she later shared with researchers at three universities.

Ashby says the most important quality in a volunteer is not expertise but {{8|patience and the patient ability to wait calmly}}. The {{9|volunteers}} records now fill eleven binders, and she hopes they will someday make dull reading: a long, uneventful list of healthy sea stars.

passages.title: The Piano Doctor
passages.text:
Ines Ortega's workshop sits above a laundromat on Delancey Street, and on most days the hum of the dryers below {{1|mixes}} with the sound of a single note being struck over and over. Ortega restores old pianos{{2|; a}} trade she learned from her uncle in Guadalajara. Most of the instruments that reach her have spent decades in church basements or in the living rooms of families who no longer play them.

Restoring a piano is slow work. Each of the eighty-eight keys must be removed and cleaned and must have {{3|their}} felt replaced, and the hammers that strike the strings often need to be reshaped by hand. {{4|Working with a small file, the felt on each hammer is shaved}} until it strikes the string at exactly the right angle. A full restoration can take Ortega three months, and she tunes each instrument several times before it leaves the shop, since new felt and freshly cleaned keys take weeks to settle.

Not every piano is worth saving. Some have cracked soundboards or warped frames, and repairing them would cost more than the instrument is worth. {{5|Nevertheless,}} Ortega rarely turns a piano away. She salvages {{6|certain useful items}} from the ones she cannot fix and uses them to repair others.

Humidity has a strong {{7|affect}} on a piano's wooden parts, so Ortega {{8|keeps her workshop at a steady temperature and runs a dehumidifier, and she checks}} the moisture level twice a day.

Last spring a church that had sold its piano decades earlier asked Ortega to find one like it. She found the original instead{{9|. In pieces,}} in her own storeroom. It took her four months to restore, and when the choir heard it again, several members said it sounded exactly as they remembered.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: task is slower than it sounds
candidates.explanation: "They are counting sea stars" and "the task is slower than it sounds" are both independent clauses, so a semicolon joins them.

A.rationale: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma form a comma splice.

C.rationale: With no punctuation, the two clauses run together.

D.rationale: "This" still begins an independent clause after only a comma.

hints: Can both parts stand alone as sentences?
candidates.remember: Join two independent clauses with a semicolon or a comma plus a conjunction.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The pronoun refers to a person and is the subject of "teaches," so "who" is correct.

A.rationale: "Which" refers to things; Ashby is a person.

B.rationale: "Whom" is an object form, but the pronoun is the subject of "teaches."

C.rationale: "Whose" shows possession and leaves "teaches" without a subject.

hints: Does the pronoun refer to a person or a thing? Is it a subject or an object?

strategy.explanation: Check person or thing, then subject or object.

candidates.remember: Who for people as subjects; which for things.

candidates.subskill: Deciding whether to keep a sentence
candidates.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.A: Kept, because it explains why the missing records were a problem.
choices.B: Kept, because it shows that the wasting disease was eventually brought under control.
choices.C: Deleted, because it repeats the information in the sentence that comes before it.
choices.D: Deleted, because it shifts the focus away from Ashby to other researchers.

candidates.evidence: She resolved that if another outbreak came, there would be a baseline
candidates.explanation: The sentence links the missing records to the consequence (losses could not be measured), which motivates Ashby's decision to create a baseline.

B.rationale: The sentence says nothing about the disease being controlled.

C.rationale: The previous sentence says records were missing; this one explains the consequence.

D.rationale: The sentence keeps the focus on why Ashby started the survey.

hints: What would be lost if the sentence were removed?

strategy.explanation: Read the paragraph without the sentence.

candidates.remember: Keep sentences that connect a cause to the decision that follows.

candidates.subskill: Unnecessary comma between a verb and its object
candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Seen a sea star" is a verb and its object, which take no punctuation between them.

A.rationale: A comma should not separate the verb "seen" from its object "a sea star."

C.rationale: A semicolon would split the clause between its verb and object.

D.rationale: A dash would separate the verb from its object.

hints: What does "seen" need right after it?

strategy.explanation: Remove punctuation between a verb and its object.

candidates.remember: No punctuation between a verb and its direct object.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: rarely count exactly the same number of animals
candidates.explanation: Because two counters rarely agree, Ashby requires a second check: cause and effect.

B.rationale: Requiring a second check responds to the counting problem; it does not contrast with it.

C.rationale: The double check is not an example of two people counting differently.

D.rationale: The rule is a response to the problem, not something similar to it.

hints: Why does Ashby require a second check?
candidates.remember: Name the relationship before choosing the transition.

candidates.subskill: Verb tense (past perfect in a past context)
candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: By the time she published her report in 2023
candidates.explanation: "By the time she published" sets a past reference point, and the tripling was complete before it, so the past perfect "had tripled" is needed.

A.rationale: "Has tripled" is present perfect, but "By the time she published" requires an action completed before a past moment.

B.rationale: The present tense does not fit an event reported in the past.

D.rationale: The future tense contradicts a change already measured.

hints: What does "By the time she published" signal about the order of events?

strategy.explanation: Match the tense to "By the time ... published."

candidates.remember: An earlier past action reported in the past takes the past perfect.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: finding she later shared with researchers at three universities
candidates.explanation: "A finding she later shared ..." renames the result described before it and is attached with a comma.

A.rationale: A period leaves "A finding she later shared ..." as a fragment with no main verb.

B.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and "a finding she later shared ..." is not one.

C.rationale: Without punctuation, the appositive runs into the clause it describes.

hints: Can "A finding she later shared ..." stand alone?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that leave a fragment.

candidates.remember: A noun phrase that renames an idea is attached with a comma, not a period.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: the most important quality in a volunteer is not expertise but
candidates.explanation: "Patience" already means the ability to wait calmly, so the extra phrase is redundant.

A.rationale: "The patient ability to wait calmly" repeats the meaning of "patience" twice.

D.rationale: This repeats the idea twice and is ungrammatical after "not expertise but."

hints: Does the phrase after the comma add new information?
candidates.remember: Cut phrases that only define the word before them.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The records belong to more than one volunteer, so the plural possessive "volunteers'" is correct.

A.rationale: The records belong to the volunteers, so a possessive is needed.

B.rationale: This is the singular possessive, but many volunteers kept the records.

C.rationale: A plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe.

hints: How many volunteers kept the records?
candidates.remember: Plural possessive: add an apostrophe after the s.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "In pieces" and "in her own storeroom" both describe where and how she found the piano; they belong in the same sentence, set off with commas.

A.rationale: A period here leaves "In pieces, in her own storeroom" as a fragment.

B.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause.

D.rationale: A semicolon after "in pieces" would leave "in her own storeroom" stranded as a fragment.

hints: Can "In pieces, in her own storeroom" stand alone?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that leave a fragment.

candidates.remember: A phrase cannot stand alone after a period.
